chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Statistical Toolkit for Spotting Reversion

lessons.title: The Z-Score: Measuring How Stretched a Price Really Is

children.text: In Chapter 1, Alpha Industries closed 15.5% below its 20-day moving average on results day. Is 15.5% below average "a lot"? For one stock, that might be a routine wobble it goes through most months. For another, it might be the biggest single deviation in five years. Comparing raw percentage deviations across different stocks is comparing apples to oranges unless you account for how much each stock normally moves in the first place. That is exactly what the z-score does, and it is the single most-used number in this entire course.

body.text: The z-score measures how many standard deviations a price currently sits away from its own recent rolling average. It converts a rupee or percentage deviation into a standardized, comparable unit of "how stretched", so a smallcap that moves 5% on an ordinary day and a stable bluechip that moves 0.5% on an ordinary day can be judged on the same scale.

body.caption: P_t is today's price, mu_t is the rolling mean over a chosen lookback window, and sigma_t is the rolling standard deviation over that same window.

children.text: Both mu_t and sigma_t are almost always computed over a rolling window, commonly 20 trading days, roughly one calendar month, rather than the stock's entire price history. Lesson 3 already established why: a raw price series is rarely stationary over its full history, a company's fair value genuinely drifts over years, so an all-time mean and an all-time standard deviation would mix together very different eras of the business. A rolling window is a practical workaround. It assumes the stock's behavior is locally stable enough, over the last month or so, to treat as approximately stationary, even if the stock's behavior five years ago looked completely different.

A 15% fall means something completely different depending on how volatile the stock normally is. A thinly traded smallcap that regularly swings 5% to 8% in a week has, statistically speaking, barely done anything unusual by falling 15%. A large, stable FMCG stock that typically moves half a percent a day falling 15% is a genuine outlier. The z-score puts both cases on the same ruler, measured in standard deviations, so "stretched" means the same thing regardless of which stock you are looking at.

body.caption: Same percentage fall, very different z-scores

children.text: Worked Example: Calculating the Z-Score by Hand
Suppose an NSE-listed stock's closing prices over the last 20 trading days have a rolling mean of ₹1,000 and a rolling standard deviation of ₹40. Today the stock closes at ₹880.

body.label: Z-score for this example
body.context: (880 - 1,000) / 40 = -120 / 40 = -3.0. The stock has closed three full standard deviations below its own 20-day average, a rare, statistically extreme move by this stock's own recent standards.

children.text: Most single-asset mean reversion strategies built in Chapter 3 and Chapter 7 use a threshold somewhere around plus or minus 2 as the point where a deviation becomes interesting, and plus or minus 2.5 to 3 as genuinely extreme. Where that threshold sits is a real design choice, set it too low and you get flooded with weak, unreliable signals, set it too high and you barely get any signals at all, a trade-off Chapter 7 covers when it comes to building entry and exit rules.

stats.label: |z| ≥ 1
stats.context: Common. Happens roughly one trading day in three under a normal distribution assumption

stats.label: |z| ≥ 2
stats.context: Notable. The most common entry threshold for single-asset reversion strategies

stats.label: |z| ≥ 3
stats.context: Rare under a normal assumption, roughly one trading day in 370

body.text: Those probabilities assume stock returns are normally distributed. Real stock returns are not. They have "fat tails", extreme moves happen noticeably more often than a normal distribution predicts, especially around results, regulatory news, and market-wide shocks. Treat the numbers above as a rough guide to rank how unusual a move is, not as a literal, reliable probability. A |z| of 3 is genuinely rare, but not nearly as rare in real Indian markets as the 0.3% figure suggests.

children.text: Once you have a daily closing price series, whether pulled from your broker's API such as Zerodha's Kite Connect, or from any historical NSE data source, the rolling z-score is a two-line calculation in pandas.

body.code:
import pandas as pd

# 'close' is a pandas Series of daily closing prices for one stock,
# indexed by date, oldest first.
window = 20

rolling_mean = close.rolling(window).mean()
rolling_std = close.rolling(window).std()

z_score = (close - rolling_mean) / rolling_std

print(z_score.tail())
body.caption: Rolling 20-day z-score for a single stock's closing price series.

body.title: 20-day rolling z-score for a hypothetical NSE stock over 60 trading days (illustrative)

body.text: Notice the z-score oscillates around zero and repeatedly pushes past 2 and -2 before pulling back. It never tells you why the price moved, only exactly how much, in standardized units. Chapter 1 already covered why you need to know the why before trading the how. This lesson is only about measuring the how, precisely and consistently, so Chapter 3 can build actual entry and exit rules on top of it.

body.title: Calculate the z-score
body.prompt: A different stock's closing prices over the last 20 trading days have a rolling mean of ₹520 and a rolling standard deviation of ₹18. Today it closes at ₹566. What is its z-score, rounded to one decimal place?
body.explanation: (566 - 520) / 18 = 46 / 18 = 2.56, which rounds to 2.6. The stock has closed more than 2.5 standard deviations above its own 20-day average, a statistically stretched move on the upside.

body.title: Which stock is most stretched?
body.question: Three NSE stocks close today. Stock P: 20-day mean ₹300, standard deviation ₹10, closes at ₹316. Stock Q: 20-day mean ₹1,200, standard deviation ₹15, closes at ₹1,242. Stock R: 20-day mean ₹75, standard deviation ₹6, closes at ₹57. Which stock is most statistically stretched from its own recent average?
options: They are all equally stretched, since none moved by more than a few tens of rupees
body.explanation: Stock P: (316-300)/10 = 1.6. Stock Q: (1,242-1,200)/15 = 2.8. Stock R: (57-75)/6 = -3.0. Ranking by absolute z-score, Stock R at 3.0 is the most stretched, even though its rupee move is the smallest of the three in absolute terms. This is exactly why z-score, not rupee or percentage change, is the right unit for comparing stretch across stocks.

cards.definition: The number of standard deviations a value sits away from its mean. In trading, how many standard deviations a price sits away from its own rolling average.
The fixed number of most recent trading days, commonly 20, used to compute a moving mean and standard deviation, rather than using the entire price history.
A measure of how much a price typically varies around its rolling mean over the lookback window, used as the unit that a z-score is measured in.
The tendency of real financial returns to produce extreme moves more often than a normal distribution would predict, meaning normal-theory probabilities for large z-scores understate real-world risk.

points: The z-score measures how many standard deviations a price sits away from its own rolling mean, converting rupee or percentage moves into a standardized, comparable unit of stretch.

The mean and standard deviation used are almost always computed over a rolling window, commonly 20 trading days, not the stock's entire history, because raw prices are not stationary over long periods.
The same percentage fall can be unremarkable for a volatile stock and extreme for a stable one. Z-score, not rupees or percentage, is the right unit for comparing stretch across different stocks.

Common thresholds are around plus or minus 2 for a notable deviation and plus or minus 2.5 to 3 for an extreme one, but real markets have fatter tails than a normal distribution, so extreme z-scores happen more often than textbook probabilities suggest.
A z-score tells you exactly how stretched a price is. It says nothing about why, which is why it is a measurement tool, not a complete trading strategy on its own.
